scenes.title: Shared services: replicate, proxy or transit
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains shared services: replicate, proxy or transit using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Replicate local application or data endpoints and assess consistency and lag
Proxy connection termination opens a distinct connection to an on-premises service
Use Transit Gateway for routed multi-VPC hybrid access with route isolation
VPC peering cannot transit another peer's VPN or Direct Connect
scenes.visual_example: An app may query a local replica, call an application proxy, or use a TGW-routed path depending on state and protocol constraints.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Validate the shared services: replicate, proxy or transit design with supported network settings, complete traffic paths and its actual failure domains.
scenes.narration: This lesson explains shared services: replicate, proxy or transit, using the actual architecture and numbered callouts on the screen. Start with the first element: Replicate local application or data endpoints and assess consistency and lag. Notice the depicted connections and boundaries; they illustrate which component owns this responsibility. Next, follow the second section: Proxy connection termination opens a distinct connection to an on-premises service. This changes how the path or control is configured, and should be checked rather than assumed. Move to the third section: Use Transit Gateway for routed multi-VPC hybrid access with route isolation. For a working design, distinguish a successful control-plane configuration from application-level reachability, security and service readiness. Now inspect the final section: VPC peering cannot transit another peer's VPN or Direct Connect. Consider a realistic architecture scenario. An app may query a local replica, call an application proxy, or use a TGW-routed path depending on state and protocol constraints. When troubleshooting, test the forward and return paths, the relevant service-specific limits and actual user traffic, then compare the result with the requirement. The key takeaway is to select the correct model and prove its behaviour under normal operation and failure.

scenes.title: VPN over Direct Connect: two addressing models
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains vpn over direct connect: two addressing models using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Public-IP Site-to-Site VPN uses public VIF reachability to AWS public VPN endpoints
Public VIF is AWS public-prefix transport, not general internet transit
Private-IP VPN uses transit VIF, Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway
Both models require underlay, IPsec overlay and application-prefix return routes

scenes.title: Multiple VPNs: active sites versus ECMP
scenes.visual_overview: The original slide explains multiple vpns: active sites versus ecmp using 4 explicitly labelled visual sections, connections, and practical limits.
visual_walkthrough: Site A and Site B advertise different prefixes and both remain active for their own networks
Equal destination prefixes on a VGW do not automatically imply equal-cost VPN sharing
Transit Gateway with compatible dynamic routing and VPN ECMP can share eligible flows
Test device independence, route withdrawals and stateful return traffic
